description: Public Administration question bank derived from FDA/SDA Examination Notes (Section 7.8). Covers meaning and scope, principles, organisation, hierarchy, delegation, coordination, accountability, transparency, good governance, e-governance, citizen-centric administration, grievance redressal, RTI Act 2005 (as amended by DPDP Act 2023) and administrative reforms.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.chapter: Public Administration - Meaning, Nature and Scope
questions.question: What is Public Administration?

options.A: The organisation and management of public policies, government programmes and public services
options.B: The management of private companies for profit
options.D: The conduct of foreign diplomacy only

questions.explanation: Public Administration is the organisation and management of public policies, government programmes and public services. It includes activities through which governments implement laws, formulate and execute policies, manage public resources and deliver services to citizens.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.chapter: Public Administration - Meaning, Nature and Scope
questions.question: What does the word 'administration' mean?

options.A: The organised process of planning, directing, coordinating and controlling people and resources to achieve specified objectives
options.C: The interpretation of statutes by courts

questions.explanation: Administration means the organised process of planning, directing, coordinating and controlling people and resources to achieve specified objectives. Public administration applies this process to public purposes and government responsibilities.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.chapter: Public Administration - Meaning, Nature and Scope
questions.question: What is the main difference between Public Administration and Private Administration?

options.A: Public Administration operates primarily for public interest and is accountable to citizens and elected institutions, while Private Administration generally operates within private ownership and commercial objectives
options.C: Public Administration does not follow any law
options.D: Private Administration is accountable to Parliament

questions.explanation: Public Administration operates primarily for public interest, is subject to constitutional and legal controls, and is accountable to citizens and elected institutions. Private Administration generally operates within private ownership and commercial or organisational objectives, though it is also subject to law and regulation.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.chapter: Public Administration - Meaning, Nature and Scope
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the nature of Public Administration?

options.A: It is both an activity and a field of study, interdisciplinary, practical, goal-oriented and service-oriented
options.B: It is purely a theoretical subject with no practical application
options.C: It is confined only to financial administration
options.D: It is a branch of pure mathematics

questions.explanation: Public Administration is both an activity and a field of study. It is interdisciplinary, practical, goal-oriented, service-oriented and concerned with policy implementation, public institutions, public finance, personnel, regulation and accountability.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.chapter: Public Administration - Meaning, Nature and Scope
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT included in the scope of Public Administration?

options.A: Personnel administration

questions.explanation: The scope of Public Administration includes organisation and management of government departments; personnel administration; financial administration; policy formulation and implementation; development administration; local government; public enterprises; law and order; public service delivery; regulatory administration; and accountability mechanisms. Private family budgeting is not part of it.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.chapter: Public Administration - Meaning, Nature and Scope
questions.question: What does POSDCORB stand for?

options.A: Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting and Budgeting
options.B: Planning, Organising, Supervising, Directing, Controlling, Reporting and Budgeting
options.C: Public, Organised, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reviewing and Budgeting
options.D: Planning, Ordering, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting and Budgeting

questions.explanation: POSDCORB is a mnemonic associated with Luther Gulick describing major functions of an executive: Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting and Budgeting.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.chapter: Public Administration - Meaning, Nature and Scope
questions.question: Who is associated with the POSDCORB approach?

options.A: Luther Gulick

questions.explanation: POSDCORB is a mnemonic associated with Luther Gulick describing major functions of an executive.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.chapter: Public Administration - Meaning, Nature and Scope
questions.question: What is the difference between the narrow and broad views of Public Administration?

options.A: The narrow view focuses mainly on the activities of the executive branch and implementation of public policy, while the broad view includes all activities connected with public affairs across legislative, executive and judicial institutions
options.B: The narrow view includes all three branches of government, while the broad view includes only the executive
options.D: The narrow view deals only with foreign affairs

questions.explanation: The narrow view focuses mainly on the activities of the executive branch and implementation of public policy. The broad view includes all activities connected with public affairs and the implementation of public policy across legislative, executive and judicial institutions.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.chapter: Public Administration - Meaning, Nature and Scope
questions.question: Why is Public Administration called an instrument of social change?

options.A: Because it implements welfare, development, education, health, infrastructure, equality and social justice programmes that can transform social and economic conditions

questions.explanation: Government administration implements welfare, development, education, health, infrastructure, equality and social justice programmes. Through these activities it can help transform social and economic conditions, subject to law, resources and public accountability.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the principle of division of work?

options.A: Dividing organisational tasks into specialised duties and assigning them to individuals or units according to competence
options.B: Giving all tasks to one person
options.C: Rotating all employees between all tasks daily

questions.explanation: Division of work means dividing organisational tasks into specialised duties and assigning them to individuals or units according to competence. Specialisation can improve skill and efficiency, but excessive fragmentation can create coordination problems.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the principle of unity of command?

options.A: Each employee should ordinarily receive instructions from one immediate superior
options.B: Each employee should receive instructions from multiple superiors simultaneously
options.C: Commands should be issued only in writing
options.D: Only the head of state can issue commands

questions.explanation: Unity of command means that each employee should ordinarily receive instructions from one immediate superior. It is intended to reduce conflicting orders and clarify responsibility.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the principle of unity of direction?

options.A: Activities having the same objective should be guided by one plan and one responsible head
options.B: All activities must be directed by the legislature
options.C: Each department must have a separate plan

questions.explanation: Unity of direction means that activities having the same objective should be guided by one plan and one responsible head.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the scalar chain or chain of command?

options.A: The formal line of authority running from the highest level to the lowest level of an organisation

questions.explanation: The scalar chain is the formal line of authority running from the highest level to the lowest level of an organisation. It establishes reporting relationships and channels for communication.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the principle of span of control?

options.A: The number of subordinates a supervisor can effectively guide and supervise
options.B: The total budget of a department
options.C: The number of laws passed by Parliament
options.D: The geographical area of a state

questions.explanation: Span of control refers to the number of subordinates a supervisor can effectively guide and supervise. The appropriate span depends on the complexity of work, geographical spread, staff competence, technology and the supervisor's capacity.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the principle of authority and responsibility?

options.A: Authority is the legitimate right to make decisions and issue instructions; responsibility is the duty to perform assigned tasks and answer for results, and both should be reasonably balanced
options.B: Authority and responsibility are unrelated concepts

questions.explanation: Authority is the legitimate right to make decisions and issue instructions; responsibility is the duty to perform assigned tasks and answer for results. Effective administration requires authority and responsibility to be reasonably balanced.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What does the principle of discipline mean in administration?

options.A: Observance of organisational rules, lawful instructions, standards of conduct and agreed procedures, applied fairly and consistently

questions.explanation: Discipline means observance of organisational rules, lawful instructions, standards of conduct and agreed procedures. It should be applied fairly and consistently.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What does the principle of equity mean in administration?

options.A: Treating employees and citizens fairly, impartially and without arbitrary discrimination
options.B: Giving all benefits to senior officers
options.C: Equal salary for all employees regardless of post

questions.explanation: Equity means treating employees and citizens fairly, impartially and without arbitrary discrimination. It supports trust and legitimacy in public institutions.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What does the principle of esprit de corps mean?

options.A: Team spirit, unity and cooperation among members of an organisation

questions.explanation: Esprit de corps means team spirit, unity and cooperation among members of an organisation. It supports morale and collective effort.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is bureaucracy in public administration?

options.A: A form of organisation based on defined offices, hierarchy, division of labour, formal rules, written records, merit-based appointment and impersonal application of rules
options.B: A system where all decisions are made by citizens directly
options.C: A form of private business management
options.D: A system with no rules and no hierarchy

questions.explanation: Bureaucracy is a form of organisation based on defined offices, hierarchy, division of labour, formal rules, written records, merit-based appointment and impersonal application of rules. Max Weber is closely associated with the ideal type of legal-rational bureaucracy.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Who is closely associated with the ideal-type theory of legal-rational bureaucracy?

options.A: Max Weber

questions.explanation: Max Weber is closely associated with the ideal type of legal-rational bureaucracy.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of Max Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy?

options.A: Impersonal, rule-based decision-making with written records and merit-based recruitment

questions.explanation: Features of Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy include a clear hierarchy of offices; defined jurisdiction and duties; written rules and records; specialisation; recruitment based on technical qualifications; career service; separation of official position from personal ownership; and impersonal, rule-based decision-making.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the human relations approach to administration?

options.A: An approach that emphasises the social and psychological dimensions of work, including employee motivation, informal groups, communication, leadership and participation
options.B: An approach that focuses only on machines and technology
options.C: An approach that ignores employees entirely
options.D: An approach based only on financial incentives

questions.explanation: The human relations approach emphasises the social and psychological dimensions of work, including employee motivation, informal groups, communication, leadership and participation. The Hawthorne studies are commonly associated with the development of this approach.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Who is commonly associated with the human relations movement and interpretation of the Hawthorne studies?

options.A: Elton Mayo

questions.explanation: Elton Mayo is commonly associated with the human relations movement and interpretation of the Hawthorne studies.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section B and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is scientific management?

options.A: An approach associated with F. W. Taylor that seeks to improve efficiency through systematic study of tasks, standardisation, work measurement, training and a considered division of managerial and operational responsibilities
options.B: An approach that relies only on intuition
options.C: An approach that ignores work measurement
options.D: An approach limited to agricultural work

questions.explanation: Scientific management, associated with F. W. Taylor, seeks to improve efficiency through systematic study of tasks, standardisation, work measurement, training and a considered division of managerial and operational responsibilities.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Who is associated with scientific management?

options.A: Frederick Winslow Taylor

questions.explanation: Frederick Winslow Taylor is associated with scientific management.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section B and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the systems approach to administration?

options.A: An approach that views an organisation as an interconnected system receiving inputs, transforming them through processes, producing outputs and outcomes, and receiving feedback from its environment
options.B: An approach that studies only individual behaviour
options.C: An approach that ignores the environment
options.D: An approach based only on legal rules

questions.explanation: The systems approach views an organisation as an interconnected system that receives inputs, transforms them through processes, produces outputs and outcomes, and receives feedback from its environment.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What does the contingency approach to administration hold?

options.A: No single administrative structure or management technique is best in every situation; design and leadership should adapt to task, environment, technology, people and circumstances
options.B: There is only one best way to organise
options.C: Environment has no effect on organisation

questions.explanation: The contingency approach holds that no single administrative structure or management technique is best in every situation. Organisational design and leadership should be adapted to the task, environment, technology, people and circumstances.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is organisation in Public Administration?

options.A: The arrangement of people, duties, authority and resources into a structured system to achieve public objectives

questions.explanation: Organisation is the arrangement of people, duties, authority and resources into a structured system to achieve public objectives. It defines roles, reporting relationships, communication channels and responsibility.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which of the following is a principle of good organisation?

options.A: Clarity of objectives, division of work, unity of command and appropriate span of control

questions.explanation: Principles of good organisation include clarity of objectives; division of work; unity of command; appropriate span of control; defined authority and responsibility; coordination; flexibility; continuity; economy; accountability; and responsiveness to public needs.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is hierarchy in administration?

options.A: The graded arrangement of positions and authority from higher to lower levels, with each level normally reporting to the level above
options.B: A system where all positions are equal
options.D: A system based only on seniority in age

questions.explanation: Hierarchy is the graded arrangement of positions and authority from higher to lower levels. Each level has defined responsibilities and normally reports to the level above it.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is an advantage of hierarchy?

options.A: It clarifies authority, reporting and responsibility, supports supervision and discipline, and provides an escalation route for decisions
options.C: It removes the need for rules

questions.explanation: Hierarchy clarifies authority, reporting and responsibility; supports supervision and discipline; provides an escalation route for decisions; and helps coordinate large organisations.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is a limitation of excessive hierarchy?

options.A: It can create delays, rigid procedures, communication distortion, excessive centralisation and reluctance to take initiative
options.B: It always improves speed of decision-making
options.C: It reduces the distance between decision-makers and citizens

questions.explanation: Excessive hierarchy can create delays, rigid procedures, communication distortion, excessive centralisation, reluctance to take initiative and distance between senior decision-makers and citizens.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is delegation of authority?

options.A: The assignment of specified tasks and decision-making authority by a superior to a subordinate while the superior retains ultimate accountability for the overall responsibility
options.B: The transfer of ownership of a department
options.C: The complete surrender of responsibility by a superior
options.D: The election of a subordinate by citizens

questions.explanation: Delegation is the assignment of specified tasks and decision-making authority by a superior to a subordinate while the superior retains ultimate accountability for the overall responsibility. The extent of delegation should be clearly defined.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What are the essential elements of delegation?

options.A: Assignment of duties, grant of adequate authority to perform those duties, and creation of accountability for performance

questions.explanation: The essential elements of delegation are assignment of duties, grant of adequate authority to perform those duties, and creation of accountability for performance. Duties without adequate authority make delegation ineffective.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Does delegation remove the superior's ultimate accountability?

options.A: No, the superior remains accountable for the overall function and for appropriate supervision
options.B: Yes, the superior has no responsibility after delegation
options.C: Yes, only the subordinate is accountable to the public
options.D: Delegation is illegal in public administration

questions.explanation: A superior may delegate the exercise of authority and performance of tasks, but remains accountable for the overall function and for appropriate supervision. The subordinate is answerable for the delegated work.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is decentralisation?

options.A: The transfer or distribution of decision-making powers and responsibilities from central authorities to lower levels, field offices or local institutions
options.B: The concentration of all power at the centre
options.D: The transfer of power to private companies

questions.explanation: Decentralisation is the transfer or distribution of decision-making powers and responsibilities from central authorities to lower levels, field offices or local institutions. It may be administrative, political or fiscal.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the difference between delegation and decentralisation?

options.A: Delegation is generally a transfer of specified authority within an organisational relationship with the superior retaining overall accountability, while decentralisation is a broader redistribution of decision-making power across levels or institutions, often supported by law
options.C: Delegation is always broader than decentralisation

questions.explanation: Delegation is generally a transfer of specified authority within an organisational relationship, with the delegating superior retaining overall accountability. Decentralisation is a broader redistribution of decision-making power across levels or institutions and may be supported by law.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is centralisation?

options.A: Concentration of decision-making authority at the higher or central level of an organisation
options.B: Distribution of all power to villages

questions.explanation: Centralisation concentrates decision-making authority at the higher or central level of an organisation. It can promote uniformity and control but may slow local responses and reduce field-level discretion.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the difference between line and staff agencies?

options.A: Line agencies perform principal operational functions and exercise direct authority in the chain of command, while staff agencies provide advice, expertise, planning or support generally without direct command
options.B: Line agencies only give advice, while staff agencies command operations
options.D: Staff agencies are always superior to line agencies

questions.explanation: Line agencies perform the principal operational functions and exercise direct authority in the chain of command. Staff agencies provide advice, expertise, planning or support to line agencies, generally without direct command over their operations unless authority is specifically assigned.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is coordination in Public Administration?

options.A: The process of harmonising the activities of different departments, officers and agencies so that their work supports common objectives and avoids duplication, conflict and gaps in service delivery
options.B: The process of punishing inefficient departments
options.C: The merger of all government departments into one
options.D: The collection of taxes from citizens

questions.explanation: Coordination is the process of harmonising the activities of different departments, officers and agencies so that their work supports common objectives and avoids duplication, conflict and gaps in service delivery.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Why is coordination necessary in government?

options.A: Public problems often cross departmental boundaries, and coordination aligns policies, budgets, schedules, information and responsibilities to reduce duplication and resolve conflicts
options.B: Because government departments are independent and never interact
options.D: Because it eliminates the need for budgets

questions.explanation: Public problems often cross departmental boundaries. Coordination aligns policies, budgets, schedules, information and responsibilities; reduces duplication; resolves conflicts; and improves the consistency of public services.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which of the following is a common method of administrative coordination?

options.A: Cabinet and committee systems, inter-departmental meetings, nodal departments, joint task forces and integrated plans and budgets

questions.explanation: Common methods of administrative coordination include Cabinet and committee systems; inter-departmental meetings; nodal departments; common guidelines; joint task forces; shared databases; integrated plans and budgets; review mechanisms; and clearly assigned lead agencies.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is vertical coordination?

options.A: Coordination that links higher and lower levels of administration, such as State headquarters, district offices, taluk offices and village-level institutions
options.B: Coordination between departments at the same level
options.C: Coordination between India and foreign countries

questions.explanation: Vertical coordination links higher and lower levels of administration, such as State headquarters, district offices, taluk offices and village-level institutions.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is horizontal coordination?

options.A: Coordination that links departments or agencies operating at the same level, such as health, education, police and revenue departments at district level
options.B: Coordination between the Centre and the States
options.C: Coordination between a superior and subordinate
options.D: Coordination between a ministry and its attached office

questions.explanation: Horizontal coordination links departments or agencies operating at the same level, such as health, education, police and revenue departments at district level.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is administrative communication?

options.A: The transmission and exchange of instructions, information, decisions, feedback and reports within government and between government and the public
options.B: The communication between private companies only
options.D: The communication between political parties only

questions.explanation: Administrative communication is the transmission and exchange of instructions, information, decisions, feedback and reports within government and between government and the public.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the difference between formal and informal communication?

options.A: Formal communication follows authorised channels and official records, while informal communication occurs through unofficial interpersonal networks
options.B: Formal communication is always verbal, informal is always written
options.C: Informal communication is illegal in government
options.D: Formal communication does not require records

questions.explanation: Formal communication follows authorised channels, official records and prescribed procedures. Informal communication occurs through unofficial interpersonal networks; it may speed information flow but should not replace required official decisions and records.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is accountability in Public Administration?

options.A: The obligation of public officials and institutions to explain and justify their decisions and actions, disclose relevant information, comply with law and accept consequences or corrective action where required
options.B: The right of officials to act without any scrutiny
options.C: The duty of citizens to obey officials
options.D: The power of officials to make arbitrary decisions

questions.explanation: Accountability is the obligation of public officials and institutions to explain and justify their decisions and actions, disclose relevant information, comply with law and accept consequences or corrective action where required.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which of the following is a major form of public accountability?

options.A: Political accountability to elected representatives, administrative accountability through supervision, legal accountability through courts, financial accountability through audit, and social accountability through citizens and media

questions.explanation: Major forms of public accountability include political accountability to elected representatives; administrative accountability through supervision and service rules; legal accountability through courts and statutory processes; financial accountability through audit and legislative committees; and social accountability through citizens, media, public hearings and community monitoring.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is transparency in administration?

options.A: Making government rules, decisions, procedures, records and performance information accessible and understandable, subject to lawful restrictions
options.D: Sharing information only with senior officials

questions.explanation: Transparency means making government rules, decisions, procedures, records and performance information accessible and understandable, subject to lawful restrictions. It reduces secrecy and enables citizens to scrutinise public action.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: How are transparency and accountability related?

options.A: Transparency provides information needed for scrutiny, while accountability requires officials to explain and answer for their conduct; transparency supports accountability but does not by itself guarantee corrective action
options.D: Transparency eliminates the need for accountability

questions.explanation: Transparency provides information needed for scrutiny; accountability requires officials to explain and answer for their conduct. Transparency supports accountability but does not by itself guarantee corrective action.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is administrative responsibility?

options.A: The duty of public servants to act lawfully, impartially, ethically and competently, use public resources properly and implement authorised policies while respecting constitutional values and citizens' rights
options.B: The duty of citizens to obey all orders
options.C: The right of officials to ignore the law
options.D: The power of officials to use public resources for personal benefit

questions.explanation: Administrative responsibility is the duty of public servants to act lawfully, impartially, ethically and competently, use public resources properly and implement authorised policies while respecting constitutional values and citizens' rights.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is administrative ethics?

options.A: Values and standards guiding public officials, including integrity, impartiality, objectivity, non-partisanship, accountability, dedication to public service, empathy and commitment to the public interest
options.B: The rules for private business profit

questions.explanation: Administrative ethics refers to values and standards guiding public officials, including integrity, impartiality, objectivity, non-partisanship, accountability, dedication to public service, empathy and commitment to the public interest.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is a conflict of interest in public service?

options.A: A situation where a public official's private, financial, family or other personal interests could improperly influence, or appear to influence, official duties
options.B: A dispute between two government departments

questions.explanation: A conflict of interest arises when a public official's private, financial, family or other personal interests could improperly influence, or appear to influence, official duties. Disclosure, recusal and compliance with conduct rules help manage such conflicts.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is a social audit?

options.A: A process through which beneficiaries and community members examine public records, expenditure, decisions and outcomes of government programmes
options.B: An audit conducted only by chartered accountants
options.C: An audit of private company accounts
options.D: A tax audit by the income tax department

questions.explanation: A social audit is a process through which beneficiaries and community members examine public records, expenditure, decisions and outcomes of government programmes. It promotes public participation and verification of whether benefits reached intended recipients.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is a Citizen's Charter?

options.A: A public statement of an organisation's services, service standards, timelines, grievance channels and responsibilities
options.C: A document listing citizens' duties only

questions.explanation: A Citizen's Charter is a public statement of an organisation's services, service standards, timelines, grievance channels and responsibilities. It informs citizens about what they can expect, though its enforceability depends on applicable law and service-guarantee frameworks.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the role of the Public Accounts Committee?

options.A: It examines audit findings and government accounts

questions.explanation: The Public Accounts Committee examines audit findings and government accounts, while departmental standing committees scrutinise the work and demands of departments.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is good governance?

options.A: The exercise of public authority in a manner that is lawful, participatory, transparent, accountable, responsive, effective, efficient, equitable and oriented towards consensus and the rule of law

questions.explanation: Good governance is the exercise of public authority in a manner that is lawful, participatory, transparent, accountable, responsive, effective, efficient, equitable and oriented towards consensus and the rule of law.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which of the following is a commonly recognised principle of good governance?

options.A: Participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, consensus orientation, equity and inclusiveness

questions.explanation: Commonly recognised principles of good governance include participation; rule of law; transparency; responsiveness; consensus orientation; equity and inclusiveness; effectiveness and efficiency; accountability; and strategic vision.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is citizen-centric administration?

options.A: Administration that designs public institutions and services around the needs, rights, convenience and dignity of people rather than the convenience of the bureaucracy
options.B: Administration designed for the convenience of bureaucrats

questions.explanation: Citizen-centric administration designs public institutions and services around the needs, rights, convenience and dignity of people rather than the convenience of the bureaucracy. It emphasises accessibility, timely delivery, clear information, inclusion and effective grievance redressal.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is responsive administration?

options.A: Administration that identifies public needs and responds within reasonable time through accessible services, communication, consultation and corrective action
options.C: Administration that responds only to senior officials
options.D: Administration that takes unlimited time to respond

questions.explanation: Responsive administration identifies public needs and responds within reasonable time through accessible services, communication, consultation and corrective action.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is inclusive administration?

options.A: Administration that ensures public policies and services are accessible to all sections, including women, children, persons with disabilities, senior citizens, disadvantaged communities and people in remote areas
options.B: Administration that serves only urban areas
options.D: Administration that serves only government employees

questions.explanation: Inclusive administration ensures that public policies and services are accessible to all sections, including women, children, persons with disabilities, senior citizens, disadvantaged communities and people in remote areas.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What does the rule of law mean in public administration?

options.A: Public power must be exercised under valid law, government and citizens are subject to law, legal procedures are followed, and arbitrary action is constrained by constitutional safeguards and judicial review
options.D: Laws apply only to private individuals

questions.explanation: The rule of law means that public power must be exercised under valid law, government and citizens are subject to law, legal procedures are followed, and arbitrary action is constrained by constitutional safeguards and judicial review.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is outcome-based administration?

options.A: Administration that evaluates public programmes by the changes they produce in people's lives, not merely by money spent or activities completed
options.B: Administration that evaluates only the money spent
options.C: Administration that evaluates only the number of activities completed

questions.explanation: Outcome-based administration evaluates public programmes by the changes they produce in people's lives, not merely by money spent or activities completed. It distinguishes inputs, processes, outputs and outcomes.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is performance measurement in government?

options.A: The use of indicators, targets, service standards, audits and evaluation to assess whether public agencies achieve their objectives efficiently and effectively
options.B: The measurement of employee height and weight
options.C: The measurement of private company profits

questions.explanation: Performance measurement uses indicators, targets, service standards, audits and evaluation to assess whether public agencies achieve their objectives efficiently and effectively.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the difference between efficiency and effectiveness?

options.A: Efficiency concerns the relationship between resources used and outputs produced, while effectiveness concerns whether the intended objectives or outcomes are achieved
options.B: Efficiency concerns outcomes, while effectiveness concerns inputs
options.C: They mean exactly the same thing

questions.explanation: Efficiency concerns the relationship between resources used and outputs produced—doing work with minimum avoidable waste. Effectiveness concerns whether the intended objectives or outcomes are achieved—doing the right work.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is e-governance?

options.A: The use of information and communication technologies, especially digital platforms and data systems, to improve government administration, public service delivery, information access, participation and accountability
options.B: The use of electronic voting machines only
options.C: The use of email by private companies only
options.D: The use of computers for entertainment

questions.explanation: E-governance is the use of information and communication technologies, especially digital platforms and data systems, to improve government administration, public service delivery, information access, participation and accountability.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What does G2C mean in the context of e-governance?

options.A: Government to Citizen

questions.explanation: The main models of e-governance are G2C (Government to Citizen), G2B (Government to Business), G2G (Government to Government) and G2E (Government to Employee).

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What does G2E mean in the context of e-governance?

options.A: Government to Employee

questions.explanation: G2E means Government to Employee, one of the main models of e-governance.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of e-governance?

options.A: Reduction of transaction time and costs, improved access to information, standardised procedures and online applications and payments
options.C: Increased need for citizens to visit offices repeatedly

questions.explanation: Benefits of e-governance include reducing transaction time and costs, improving access to information, standardising procedures, enabling online applications and payments, creating digital records, improving tracking and supporting data-informed decisions.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which of the following is a limitation or risk of e-governance?

options.A: Digital exclusion, poor connectivity, low digital literacy, cybersecurity threats, privacy risks, inaccurate data and algorithmic bias

questions.explanation: Limitations and risks of e-governance include digital exclusion, poor connectivity, low digital literacy, language barriers, cybersecurity threats, privacy risks, inaccurate data, system outages, algorithmic bias and over-reliance on online-only processes.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the digital divide?

options.A: The gap between people or regions in access to digital devices, internet connectivity, digital skills, accessible interfaces and the ability to use digital services effectively
options.B: The difference between two computer screens
options.C: The gap between urban and rural taxes
options.D: The division of a ministry into departments

questions.explanation: The digital divide is the gap between people or regions in access to digital devices, internet connectivity, digital skills, accessible interfaces and the ability to use digital services effectively.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the difference between digitisation, digitalisation and digital transformation?

options.A: Digitisation converts analogue information into digital form; digitalisation uses digital tools to improve existing processes; digital transformation redesigns services, workflows and institutions around digital capabilities and user needs
options.B: All three terms mean the same thing
options.C: Digitisation refers to institutional redesign, while digital transformation refers to converting paper to digital form
options.D: Digitalisation refers to building new institutions

questions.explanation: Digitisation converts analogue information into digital form. Digitalisation uses digital tools to improve existing processes. Digital transformation redesigns services, workflows and institutions around digital capabilities and user needs.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What was the purpose of the National e-Governance Plan (NeGP)?

options.A: To make government services accessible to citizens through common service delivery outlets and ensure efficiency, transparency and reliability at affordable cost
options.B: To replace all government employees with computers
options.D: To abolish the use of the internet in government

questions.explanation: The National e-Governance Plan (NeGP), approved in 2006, sought to make government services accessible to citizens through common service delivery outlets and to ensure efficiency, transparency and reliability at affordable cost. Later initiatives built on and expanded this framework.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: In which year was the National e-Governance Plan (NeGP) approved?
questions.explanation: The National e-Governance Plan (NeGP) was approved in 2006.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the Digital India programme?

options.A: A Government of India programme launched in 2015 to transform India into a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy
options.D: A programme to reduce internet access

questions.explanation: Digital India is a Government of India programme launched in 2015 to transform India into a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy. Its broad focus includes digital infrastructure, governance and services on demand, and digital empowerment of citizens.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: In which year was the Digital India programme launched?
questions.explanation: Digital India was launched in 2015 to transform India into a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is a Common Service Centre (CSC)?

options.A: A service-delivery access point that provides digital and other government, financial, educational and utility services, particularly to people who may not be able to access online systems independently
options.B: A centre for training civil servants
options.D: A centre for collecting taxes only

questions.explanation: A Common Service Centre (CSC) is a service-delivery access point that provides digital and other government, financial, educational and utility services, particularly to people who may not be able to access online systems independently.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the Karnataka Sakala initiative?

options.A: Karnataka's time-bound public service delivery framework under the Karnataka Guarantee of Services to Citizens Act, 2011

questions.explanation: Sakala is Karnataka's time-bound public service delivery framework under the Karnataka Guarantee of Services to Citizens Act, 2011. It provides notified services with prescribed timelines and a mechanism for citizens to seek remedies where services are delayed or denied, subject to the Act and rules.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the purpose of digital identity and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) in administration?

options.A: To authenticate beneficiaries and transfer eligible benefits directly to bank accounts, subject to applicable law, data protection, exclusion safeguards and grievance procedures
options.D: To collect additional taxes from citizens

questions.explanation: Digital identity and payment infrastructure can help authenticate beneficiaries and transfer eligible benefits directly to bank accounts. Their use must comply with applicable law, data protection, exclusion safeguards and grievance procedures.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is a public grievance?

options.A: A complaint by a citizen about delay, denial, deficiency, unfair treatment, corruption, maladministration or failure in a public service or government programme
options.B: A petition filed in a court of law
options.C: A request for information under the RTI Act

questions.explanation: A public grievance is a complaint by a citizen about delay, denial, deficiency, unfair treatment, corruption, maladministration or failure in a public service or government programme.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which of the following is a stage of an effective grievance redressal system?

options.A: Accessible complaint registration, acknowledgement and tracking, investigation, time-bound decision, communication of reasons and analysis of recurring complaints

questions.explanation: The main stages of an effective grievance redressal system include accessible complaint registration; acknowledgement and tracking; assignment to a responsible authority; investigation; time-bound decision; communication of reasons and outcome; appeal or review where available; and analysis of recurring complaints to improve systems.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What does CPGRAMS stand for?

options.A: Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System
options.B: Central Public Grievance Registration and Management System
options.C: Citizen Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring Scheme
options.D: Centralised Programme for Grievance Redress and Management Services

questions.explanation: CPGRAMS is the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System, an online platform of the Government of India for lodging and monitoring grievances relating to participating Central Government departments and organisations. It is not a substitute for every statutory appeal or court remedy.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the difference between a grievance and an RTI application?

options.A: A grievance seeks action or redressal of a problem, while an RTI application seeks access to information held by or under the control of a public authority
options.B: A grievance seeks information, while an RTI application seeks action
options.D: An RTI application automatically grants the substantive service requested

questions.explanation: A grievance seeks action or redressal of a problem. An RTI application seeks access to information held by or under the control of a public authority. RTI can help a citizen obtain records relevant to a grievance, but it does not itself compel the authority to grant the substantive service or remedy.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is an ombudsman?

options.A: An independent or specially designated authority that investigates complaints about maladministration or specified institutional conduct and may recommend or direct remedies according to the law creating the office
options.B: A judge of the Supreme Court

questions.explanation: An ombudsman is an independent or specially designated authority that investigates complaints about maladministration or specified institutional conduct and may recommend or direct remedies according to the law creating the office.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the Lokayukta institution?

options.A: A State-level anti-corruption and grievance-related institution established under State law to investigate allegations against public functionaries within its statutory jurisdiction

questions.explanation: The Lokayukta is a State-level anti-corruption and grievance-related institution established under State law to investigate allegations against public functionaries within its statutory jurisdiction. Karnataka has a Lokayukta institution under the Karnataka Lokayukta Act, 1984.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Under which Act is the Karnataka Lokayukta established?

options.A: Karnataka Lokayukta Act, 1984
options.D: Karnataka Guarantee of Services to Citizens Act, 2011

questions.explanation: Karnataka has a Lokayukta institution under the Karnataka Lokayukta Act, 1984, as amended.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section H and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the role of the Karnataka Lokayukta?

options.A: It investigates allegations of corruption and maladministration against public servants within the scope of the Karnataka Lokayukta Act, 1984 and applicable amendments
options.B: It conducts elections to the State Legislature
options.C: It issues currency notes for Karnataka
options.D: It appoints judges to the High Court

questions.explanation: The Karnataka Lokayukta investigates allegations of corruption and maladministration against public servants within the scope of the Karnataka Lokayukta Act, 1984 and applicable amendments. Its jurisdiction, procedure and powers must be understood from the current State law.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the Lokpal?

options.A: The national-level anti-corruption ombudsman established under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013
options.B: A State-level institution established under State laws
options.C: A department of the Reserve Bank of India

questions.explanation: The Lokpal is the national-level anti-corruption ombudsman established under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. Lokayuktas are State-level institutions established under State laws, with jurisdiction and powers determined by the relevant State legislation.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Under which Act is the Lokpal established?

options.A: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013

questions.explanation: The Lokpal is the national-level anti-corruption ombudsman established under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the Karnataka Sakala grievance mechanism?

options.A: Under the Sakala framework, a citizen may use the prescribed application and appeal or compensation mechanisms where a notified service is not delivered within the stipulated time or is improperly denied
options.B: A mechanism for filing criminal cases
options.C: A mechanism for appealing to the Supreme Court
options.D: A mechanism for requesting information under the RTI Act

questions.explanation: Under the Sakala framework, a citizen may use the prescribed application and appeal or compensation mechanisms where a notified service is not delivered within the stipulated time or is improperly denied. The exact procedure depends on the current Act, rules and service notification.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: When did the Right to Information Act, 2005 receive Presidential assent?

options.A: 15 June 2005

questions.explanation: The RTI Act, 2005 received Presidential assent on 15 June 2005. Most of its provisions came into force on 12 October 2005.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: When did most provisions of the Right to Information Act, 2005 come into force?

options.A: 12 October 2005

questions.explanation: Most provisions of the RTI Act, 2005 came into force on 12 October 2005.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section I and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the objective of the Right to Information Act, 2005?

options.A: To provide a practical regime for citizens to secure access to information under the control of public authorities, promote transparency and accountability, contain corruption and strengthen democracy
options.C: To restrict citizens' access to government records

questions.explanation: The RTI Act provides a practical regime for citizens to secure access to information under the control of public authorities, promote transparency and accountability, contain corruption and strengthen democracy.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Who can seek information under the RTI Act, 2005?

options.A: A citizen of India

questions.explanation: A citizen of India has the right to request information under Section 3. The Act does not confer the same statutory right on non-citizens.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Under which Section of the RTI Act is a 'public authority' defined?

options.A: Section 2(h)

questions.explanation: Under Section 2(h), a public authority includes an authority, body or institution of self-government established or constituted by or under the Constitution, by a law made by Parliament or a State Legislature, or by government notification or order; it also includes bodies owned, controlled or substantially financed by government and qualifying non-government organisations substantially financed directly or indirectly by government funds.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Under which Section of the RTI Act is 'information' defined?

options.A: Section 2(f)

questions.explanation: Section 2(f) defines information broadly to include records, documents, memos, e-mails, opinions, advice, press releases, circulars, orders, logbooks, contracts, reports, papers, samples and data material in any electronic form, and information relating to a private body that a public authority can access under another law.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What does the 'right to information' include under Section 2(j) of the RTI Act?

options.A: The right to inspect works, documents and records; take notes, extracts or certified copies; take certified samples of material; and obtain information in electronic form
options.B: The right to demand new information that does not exist
options.C: The right to compel the PIO to conduct research
options.D: The right to seek explanations not held on record

questions.explanation: Under Section 2(j), the right to information includes the right to inspect works, documents and records; take notes, extracts or certified copies; take certified samples of material; and obtain information in electronic form or as printouts where stored electronically.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Who is a Public Information Officer (PIO) under the RTI Act?

options.A: An officer designated by a public authority under Section 5 to receive and process RTI requests and provide information or issue a lawful response
options.B: A judge of the Information Commission
options.D: A citizen who files an RTI application

questions.explanation: A Public Information Officer (PIO) is an officer designated by a public authority under Section 5 to receive and process RTI requests and provide information or issue a lawful response.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the normal time limit for responding to an RTI application under Section 7(1)?

options.A: 30 days

questions.explanation: Under Section 7(1), information must ordinarily be provided within 30 days of receipt of the request or the request must be rejected with reasons under the Act.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section I and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the time limit for providing information concerning the life or liberty of a person under the RTI Act?

options.A: 48 hours

questions.explanation: The information must be provided within 48 hours of receipt of the request under the proviso to Section 7(1).
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section I and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the time limit when an RTI application is submitted through an Assistant Public Information Officer (APIO)?

options.A: An additional five days are added to the period for responding under Section 5(2)
options.B: The time limit is reduced to 15 days
options.C: The time limit is extended to 60 days

questions.explanation: An additional five days are added to the period for responding under Section 5(2) when an RTI application is submitted through an Assistant Public Information Officer.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What happens if a public authority fails to respond within the prescribed time under the RTI Act?

options.A: It is treated as a deemed refusal under Section 7(2), and the applicant may file a first appeal under Section 19(1)
options.D: The applicant must file a fresh application

questions.explanation: Under Section 7(2), failure to give a decision within the time specified is treated as a deemed refusal. The applicant may file a first appeal under Section 19(1).

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the application fee prescribed under the Central Government RTI Rules?

options.A: ₹10 for a Central public authority application, subject to exemptions and different rules for States

questions.explanation: The Central Government RTI Rules prescribe a fee of ₹10 for a Central public authority application, subject to exemptions and different rules for States. Karnataka applicants should follow the current Karnataka RTI Rules and notified payment methods rather than assuming the Central fee applies unchanged.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Is a person below the poverty line required to pay the prescribed fee under the RTI Act?

options.A: No, under Section 7(5) a person below the poverty line is not required to pay the prescribed fee, subject to the rules and proof requirements
options.B: Yes, everyone must pay the fee
options.C: Yes, but only half the fee

questions.explanation: Under Section 7(5), a person below the poverty line is not required to pay the prescribed fee, subject to the rules and proof requirements applicable to the request.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What happens if a public authority misses the statutory response deadline under the RTI Act?

options.A: Under Section 7(6), information must be provided free of charge
options.C: The applicant must pay double the fee

questions.explanation: Under Section 7(6), information must be provided free of charge where the public authority fails to comply with the time limits specified in Section 7(1).

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the first appeal under the RTI Act?

options.A: An appeal to an officer senior in rank to the PIO within the same public authority, ordinarily within 30 days under Section 19(1)
options.B: An appeal directly to the Supreme Court
options.C: An appeal to the President of India
options.D: An appeal to the Information Commission

questions.explanation: Under Section 19(1), a person who does not receive a decision within the prescribed time or is aggrieved by a PIO decision may appeal to an officer senior in rank to the PIO within the same public authority, ordinarily within 30 days. The appellate authority may admit a delayed appeal for sufficient cause.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section I and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the second appeal under the RTI Act?

options.A: An appeal to the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission, as applicable, within 90 days under Section 19(3)
options.B: An appeal to the same PIO again
options.C: An appeal to the High Court only

questions.explanation: Under Section 19(3), a second appeal lies to the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission, as applicable, within 90 days from the date on which the first appellate decision should have been made or was received. Delay may be condoned for sufficient cause.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section I and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the time limit for deciding a first appeal under the RTI Act?

options.A: Within 30 days of receipt, extendable to a total of 45 days for reasons recorded in writing under Section 19(6)

questions.explanation: A first appeal should be disposed of within 30 days of receipt, extendable to a total of 45 days for reasons recorded in writing under Section 19(6).

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the time limit for deciding a second appeal under the RTI Act?

options.A: Within 90 days, with extension for reasons recorded in writing under Section 19(9)

questions.explanation: A second appeal should be disposed of within 90 days, with extension for reasons recorded in writing under Section 19(9).

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which of the following is a major exemption under Section 8 of the RTI Act?

options.A: Information affecting sovereignty and security, information forbidden by a court, parliamentary privilege, commercial confidence and trade secrets, fiduciary information and personal information protected as amended
options.B: All information relating to government expenditure
options.C: All information relating to citizens' welfare schemes
options.D: All information published on government websites

questions.explanation: Exemptions under Section 8 include information affecting sovereignty and security; information forbidden by a court or whose disclosure may constitute contempt; parliamentary or legislative privilege; commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property where protected interests would be harmed, subject to public-interest override; fiduciary information, subject to public-interest override; information received in confidence from foreign governments; information endangering life or safety or identifying confidential sources; information impeding investigation or prosecution; Cabinet papers subject to statutory conditions; and personal information protected by the Act as amended.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the public-interest override under Section 8(2) of the RTI Act?

options.A: A public authority may allow access to exempt information where public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interests, subject to the Act and other applicable legal restrictions
options.B: All exempt information must always be disclosed
options.C: All exempt information must always be withheld
options.D: The public interest override applies only to personal information

questions.explanation: Under Section 8(2), a public authority may allow access to exempt information where public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interests, subject to the Act and other applicable legal restrictions.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the severability principle under Section 10 of the RTI Act?

options.A: If only part of a record is exempt, the non-exempt portion may be disclosed after severing or redacting the exempt portion
options.B: If any part of a record is exempt, the entire record must be withheld
options.C: Severability applies only to personal information
options.D: Severability means the applicant must file separate applications for each part

questions.explanation: If only part of a record is exempt, the non-exempt portion may be disclosed after severing or redacting the exempt portion, with the applicant informed of the decision and reasons as required by law.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the role of the Central Information Commission (CIC)?

options.A: It hears second appeals and complaints relating to Central public authorities, exercises powers under the RTI Act, may require steps to secure compliance, and can impose statutory penalties on PIOs
options.B: It conducts elections to the Lok Sabha
options.D: It appoints judges to the Supreme Court

questions.explanation: The CIC hears second appeals and complaints relating to Central public authorities, exercises powers under the RTI Act, may require steps to secure compliance, and can impose statutory penalties on PIOs in appropriate cases.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the role of the Karnataka State Information Commission?

options.A: It hears second appeals and complaints concerning public authorities within the State's jurisdiction and exercises powers under the RTI Act, including inquiry and penalty powers
options.B: It hears appeals from the Supreme Court
options.C: It issues directions to the President of India
options.D: It conducts elections to the State Legislature

questions.explanation: The Karnataka State Information Commission hears second appeals and complaints concerning public authorities within the State's jurisdiction and exercises powers under the RTI Act, including inquiry and penalty powers as prescribed by law.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What penalty can be imposed on a PIO under Section 20 of the RTI Act?

options.A: ₹250 per day for delay, subject to a maximum of ₹25,000, where the statutory grounds are established
options.B: ₹500 per day with no maximum limit
options.C: ₹1,000 per day subject to a maximum of ₹50,000
options.D: Imprisonment for one year without any fine

questions.explanation: The Information Commission may impose a penalty of ₹250 per day for delay, subject to a maximum of ₹25,000, where the statutory grounds are established, such as refusal without reasonable cause, malafide denial, knowingly incorrect or misleading information, destruction of information or obstruction. The PIO must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section I and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Can the Information Commission recommend disciplinary action against a PIO?

options.A: Yes, under Section 20(2), where the Commission is of the opinion that the PIO has persistently and without reasonable cause committed specified misconduct, it may recommend disciplinary action under the applicable service rules
options.B: No, the Commission can only impose fines
options.C: Yes, but only the Supreme Court can recommend disciplinary action
options.D: No, disciplinary action can only be taken by the PIO's family

questions.explanation: Under Section 20(2), where the Commission is of the opinion that the PIO has persistently and without reasonable cause committed specified misconduct, it may recommend disciplinary action under the applicable service rules.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the proactive disclosure obligation under Section 4 of the RTI Act?

options.A: Public authorities must maintain records appropriately and proactively publish specified organisational, functional, decision-making, financial and other information so that citizens need not file RTI applications for routine information
options.B: Public authorities must publish all information only when an RTI application is filed
options.C: Public authorities must destroy old records every year
options.D: Public authorities must publish only information relating to foreign affairs

questions.explanation: Public authorities must maintain records appropriately and proactively publish specified organisational, functional, decision-making, financial and other information so that citizens need not file RTI applications for routine information. The disclosures should be updated at regular intervals.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Is a PIO generally required to create new information, conduct research or draw inferences under the RTI Act?

options.A: No, the Act provides access to information that exists and is held by or under the control of a public authority; a PIO is not generally required to create new information or provide explanations not held on record
options.B: Yes, the PIO must always create new information
options.C: Yes, but only for Central Government authorities
options.D: Yes, but only for State Government authorities

questions.explanation: The Act provides access to information that exists and is held by or under the control of a public authority. A PIO is not generally required to create new information, conduct research, draw inferences or provide explanations that are not held on record.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the relationship between the RTI Act and the Official Secrets Act, 1923?

options.A: Section 22 of the RTI Act gives the RTI Act overriding effect over inconsistent provisions of the Official Secrets Act and other laws, subject to the RTI Act's own exemptions and restrictions
options.B: The Official Secrets Act completely overrides the RTI Act
options.C: Both Acts are identical in scope
options.D: The RTI Act does not apply to any matter covered by the Official Secrets Act

questions.explanation: Section 22 of the RTI Act gives the RTI Act overriding effect over inconsistent provisions of the Official Secrets Act and other laws, subject to the RTI Act's own exemptions and restrictions.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the relationship between the RTI Act and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023?

options.A: The DPDP Act, 2023 amended the personal-information exemption in Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act; for examination purposes, the amended statutory text in force must be used
options.B: The DPDP Act repealed the RTI Act entirely
options.C: The RTI Act overrides the DPDP Act completely
options.D: The DPDP Act has no effect on the RTI Act

questions.explanation: The DPDP Act, 2023 amended the personal-information exemption in Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act. For examination purposes, use the amended statutory text in force, not older notes reproducing the pre-amendment wording. The interaction of privacy and transparency must be assessed under the current law and constitutional principles.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which Act establishes the right to information in India?

options.A: The Right to Information Act, 2005
options.C: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

questions.explanation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 establishes the right to information in India.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Which amendment to the RTI Act relates to the personal-information exemption under Section 8(1)(j)?

options.A: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
options.D: The Karnataka Guarantee of Services to Citizens Act, 2011

questions.explanation: The DPDP Act, 2023 amended the personal-information exemption in Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act. Always study the current bare Act and applicable rules, not outdated summaries.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section I and Important legal update

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What are administrative reforms?

options.A: Planned changes in government structures, procedures, personnel systems, technology, accountability and service delivery intended to improve efficiency, effectiveness, integrity, responsiveness and public trust
options.B: Changes made only to private companies
options.D: Increases in the number of government holidays

questions.explanation: Administrative reforms are planned changes in government structures, procedures, personnel systems, technology, accountability and service delivery intended to improve efficiency, effectiveness, integrity, responsiveness and public trust.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Why are administrative reforms necessary?

options.A: They address delays, red tape, corruption, duplication, weak accountability, outdated procedures, poor service quality, skills gaps, fiscal constraints and changing public expectations

questions.explanation: Administrative reforms are necessary because they address delays, red tape, corruption, duplication, weak accountability, outdated procedures, poor service quality, skills gaps, fiscal constraints and changing public expectations.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: When was the First Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) established?

options.A: January 1966

questions.explanation: The First Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) was established in January 1966 to examine the public administration of India and recommend reforms for improving efficiency and standards. It submitted 20 reports covering major areas of administration.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section J and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: How many reports did the First Administrative Reforms Commission submit?

options.A: 20 reports

questions.explanation: The First Administrative Reforms Commission submitted 20 reports covering major areas of administration.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: When was the Second Administrative Reforms Commission constituted?
questions.explanation: The Second ARC was constituted in 2005 under the chairmanship of Veerappa Moily. It submitted 15 reports on subjects including ethics, local governance, e-governance, financial management, citizen-centric administration, personnel administration and crisis management.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section J and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: Who chaired the Second Administrative Reforms Commission?

options.A: Veerappa Moily

questions.explanation: The Second ARC was constituted in 2005 under the chairmanship of Veerappa Moily.
questions.source: Public Administration Notes, Section J and Section K

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: How many reports did the Second Administrative Reforms Commission submit?

options.A: 15 reports

questions.explanation: The Second ARC submitted 15 reports on subjects including ethics, local governance, e-governance, financial management, citizen-centric administration, personnel administration and crisis management.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the significance of the Second ARC report titled 'Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance'?

options.A: It examined how transparency and access to information could strengthen accountability and improve governance
options.B: It recommended the repeal of the RTI Act
options.C: It dealt only with foreign policy
options.D: It proposed the abolition of the Information Commissions

questions.explanation: The Second ARC's report titled 'Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance' examined how transparency and access to information could strengthen accountability and improve governance.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is the concept of 'minimum government, maximum governance'?

options.A: A reform-oriented expression emphasising simpler procedures, reduced unnecessary controls, improved public service delivery, technology-enabled administration and greater focus on outcomes
options.B: A constitutional doctrine mandating the abolition of government
options.D: A scheme to reduce the number of citizens

questions.explanation: It is a reform-oriented expression emphasising simpler procedures, reduced unnecessary controls, improved public service delivery, technology-enabled administration and greater focus on outcomes. It is a policy slogan rather than a constitutional doctrine.

questions.subject: Public Administration
questions.question: What is mission-mode administration?

options.A: Organising a programme around clearly defined goals, timelines, leadership, resources, measurable milestones and monitoring mechanisms to achieve specific public outcomes
